easy.explanation: The king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen.
easy.q: Who came with the king to banquet with Esther?

answers: What her petition and request were
easy.explanation: The king asked Esther what her petition and request were.
easy.q: What did the king ask Esther?

answers: Her life and the lives of her people
easy.explanation: Esther asked that her life and the lives of her people be given to her.
easy.q: Whose lives did Esther ask the king to save?

answers: Because she and her people had been sold to be destroyed
Because the king had left the banquet
Because Haman wanted to become king
medium.explanation: Esther said, “For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed.”
medium.q: Why did Esther say she was making her request?

answers: I would have left the palace
medium.explanation: Esther said she would have remained silent if they had merely been sold as bondmen and bondwomen.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “I had held my tongue” mean?

answers: The decree called for destruction, not merely slavery
medium.explanation: Esther emphasized that they were sold to be destroyed, slain, and to perish.
medium.q: What difference did Esther make between slavery and the decree against her people?

answers: As a plea for her life and the lives of her people
As a demand for half the kingdom
As a request to punish Mordecai
challenge.explanation: She first asked that her life and her people’s lives be given to her.
challenge.q: How did Esther first present her request before naming the guilty person?

answers: It was a threat to the existence of an entire people
challenge.explanation: Esther described a plan to destroy, slay, and cause her people to perish.
challenge.q: What can be inferred about the decree from Esther’s words?

answers: It showed that slavery was desirable
It proved that Haman was a servant
It showed that the actual decree was far worse than slavery
challenge.explanation: She said she would have held her tongue if the people had merely been sold as bondmen and bondwomen.
challenge.q: Why did mentioning slavery strengthen Esther’s argument?

easy.explanation: The king asked, “Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?”
easy.q: Who asked Esther who was responsible for the decree?

easy.explanation: Esther said, “The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.”
easy.q: Whom did Esther identify as the adversary and enemy?

easy.explanation: The KJV says that Haman was afraid before the king and the queen.
easy.q: How did Haman react after Esther identified him?

answers: Who was responsible and where he could be found
Who had spoken well of the king
medium.explanation: The king wanted to identify the person who had dared to do such a thing.
medium.q: What did the king want to know when he asked, “Who is he, and where is he”?

medium.explanation: Haman became terrified when Esther exposed him before the king.
medium.q: What does “was afraid” mean in this scene?

answers: From the banquet to the person responsible for the plot
From Haman to building the palace
medium.explanation: The king moved from hearing Esther’s request to asking who had caused the danger.
medium.q: How did Esther’s words change the focus of the conversation?

answers: He was both king and servant
He was called an adversary and a wicked man while standing before the king
He was both joyful and peaceful
challenge.explanation: Esther called Haman “the adversary and enemy” and “this wicked Haman.”
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in Esther’s description of Haman?

answers: He did not understand her words
He recognized that the accusation placed him in danger
He wanted the banquet to continue
challenge.explanation: Haman was afraid immediately after Esther identified him before the king and queen.
challenge.q: What does Haman’s fear suggest about Esther’s accusation?

answers: It gives Esther the opportunity to identify Haman directly
challenge.explanation: The king’s question allows Esther to reveal that Haman is the enemy.
challenge.q: Why is the king’s question, “Who is he,” important to the story?

paragraphs.title: The King's Anger and Haman's Doom

easy.explanation: The king arose from the banquet and went into the palace garden.
easy.q: Where did the king go in his wrath?

easy.explanation: Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen.
easy.q: What did Haman ask Esther for?

answers: Haman fallen upon the bed where Esther was
easy.explanation: The king saw Haman fallen upon the bed whereon Esther was.
easy.q: What did the king see when he returned to the banquet place?

answers: Because he wanted to invite Mordecai
medium.explanation: The KJV says that the king went into the garden “in his wrath.”
medium.q: Why did the king go into the palace garden?

answers: Good fortune was coming to him
Punishment and danger had been decided against him
medium.explanation: Haman understood that the king had determined evil, or punishment, against him.
medium.q: What does the phrase “there was evil determined against him” mean?

answers: She had exposed him and might plead for him
She was waiting in the garden
medium.explanation: After Esther accused him, Haman pleaded with her for his life.
medium.q: Why did Haman ask Esther for his life?

answers: The king’s departure from the banquet alone
Esther’s accusation and the king’s wrath
challenge.explanation: After Esther exposed him and the king left in wrath, Haman saw that evil had been determined against him.
challenge.q: What caused Haman to realize that his end was near?

answers: As an attempt to force the queen
As a customary request for forgiveness
As an attempt to help Esther
challenge.explanation: The king asked, “Will he force the queen also before me in the house?”
challenge.q: How did the king interpret Haman’s position on Esther’s bed?

answers: The king returns, Haman pleads, and the king leaves
Haman falls, the king leaves, and Haman is pardoned
The king leaves in wrath, Haman pleads, and the king returns
challenge.explanation: The king first leaves for the garden, Haman pleads for his life, and then the king returns.
challenge.q: Which sequence correctly follows the events in these verses?

easy.explanation: Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, told the king about the gallows.
easy.q: Who told the king about the gallows?

easy.explanation: Harbonah said that Haman had made the gallows for Mordecai.
easy.q: For whom had Haman made the gallows?
What did the king command to be done to Haman?

answers: Mordecai had spoken good for the king
medium.explanation: Harbonah identified Mordecai as the one “who had spoken good for the king.”
medium.q: What good thing about Mordecai did Harbonah mention?

medium.explanation: The king’s wrath was pacified, meaning that his anger subsided.
medium.q: In the final verse, what does “the king’s wrath pacified” mean?

medium.explanation: Harbonah described the gallows as fifty cubits high.
medium.q: How high were the gallows Haman had made?

answers: Haman was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai
Mordecai was hanged on the gallows Haman had prepared
The gallows were moved into the palace garden
challenge.explanation: Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.
challenge.q: What is the central connection between the gallows and Haman’s fate?

answers: It caused the king to cancel the banquet
It reminded the king that Mordecai had spoken good for him, unlike Haman’s actions
It proved that Mordecai had built the gallows
challenge.explanation: Harbonah mentioned Mordecai’s loyalty while pointing out the gallows Haman had made against him.
challenge.q: How did remembering Mordecai help lead to the king’s decision?

answers: The punishment was viewed as ending the king’s anger
challenge.explanation: The chapter ends by saying that the king’s wrath was pacified after Haman was hanged.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the king’s wrath being pacified after Haman was hanged?
